summary_html: A **child is removed without exigency or warrant**, violating constitutional rights. Federal courts treat such removals as seizures under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, actionable via §1983.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — limits removals to lawful emergencies and requires judicial review  
- **U.S. Constitution (4th & 14th Amendments)** — protects family integrity; requires due process

primary_citations.citation_text: Texas - Texas Family Code Chapter 261 (Investigation of Report of Child Abuse or Neglect)
Texas - Texas Family Code Chapter 262 (Procedures in Suit by Governmental Entity to Protect Health and Safety of Child)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Fabricating evidence of child sexual abuse that causes a child's removal violates the parents' substantive due process right to family integrity and shocks the conscience.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling Fifth Circuit authority when a Texas removal rests on manufactured evidence.
key_cases.quote: the district court was correct in holding that a teacher's fabrication of sexual abuse against a student's father shocks the contemporary conscience

key_cases.case_name: In re Texas Department of Family & Protective Services
key_cases.holding: The mass removal of children from the YFZ Ranch was not warranted on the evidence, because Chapter 262 requires danger to the individual child and the Family Code gives courts ample authority to protect children without separating them from their parents.
key_cases.relevance: The Texas Supreme Court's controlling application of Family Code §§ 262.101-.201 at this node: danger must be proved as to the particular child, and the court must use the Code's lesser alternatives — orders restraining a party, removing the alleged perpetrator, or assisting the investigation — before separating a family.
key_cases.quote: the Family Code gives the district court broad authority to protect children short of separating them from their parents and placing them in foster care

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Texas child-protection caseworkers who remove children are entitled to qualified, not absolute, immunity; on these facts the workers' temporary warrantless removal was objectively reasonable and violated no clearly established right, so qualified immunity applied.
key_cases.relevance: The line Gates, Roe and Wernecke are drawn from; any § 1983 unlawful-removal claim against Texas CPS staff begins here and must clear the clearly-established prong.
key_cases.quote: In these circumstances, we think that appellants’ actions in temporarily removing the children from the home were objectively reasonable, and as a matter of law violated no clearly established right.

key_cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The government may not seize a child from his parents absent a court order, parental consent or exigent circumstances, exigency meaning reasonable cause to believe the child is in imminent danger of physical or sexual abuse; an uncorroborated anonymous tip will rarely suffice. Because that law was not clearly established when these events occurred, every individual defendant received qualified immunity and summary judgment was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the elements of an unlawful-removal claim, while its own disposition shows how completely qualified immunity absorbs conduct that predates a clear rule.
key_cases.quote: an anonymous tip regarding child abuse will rarely be sufficient to justify the seizure of a child

key_cases.case_name: Roe v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: A CPS caseworker's visual body-cavity search of a child raised a Fourth Amendment claim, and in non-exigent circumstances the worker must obtain a warrant or court order rather than proceed on a parent's silence; a parent's consent to an investigative home interview is not consent to such a search, and consent to entry may be revoked. Because those rights were not clearly established, the worker received qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: A § 1983 claim survived on the merits but died on qualified immunity, which is the realistic outcome pattern for Texas investigative-misconduct claims.
key_cases.quote: In non-exigent circumstances, the worker then has time to obtain a warrant either personally to conduct a visual body cavity search or to have a physician perform it.
